newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: YUGO SHOULD TARGET 1.0 MLN T WHEAT EXPORTS-CHAMBER.
newsitem.headline: YUGO SHOULD TARGET 1.0 MLN T WHEAT EXPORTS-CHAMBER.

text.p: Yugoslavia has sufficient capacities and should aim to become a permanent exporter of around one million tonnes of wheat per year, a Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce official said on Thursday.

"We should advocate exports of raw materials also and not just products of a higher degree of processing for which we are still not prepared," Milan Prostran, secretary of the chamber's Association for Agriculture, told Reuters in an interview.
While Yugoslavia needed much work to raise exports of goods of a higher degree of processing, primary agricultural produce is always competitive on world markets.
"Primary products are our greater reality and we must go for very organized exports of these to markets that are close to us or have the demand," Prostran said.

He said the state should "untie its bags" to stimulate such export programmes that could become a more stable source of funds to reinvest in the ailing farm sector, exhausted after nearly four years of international isolation.

According to the chamber's latest data from the field, around 3.1 million tonnes of wheat were reaped from some 817,000 hectares under the crop in one of the longest and most difficult harvests in decades.
"The wheat at the start of harvest in early July was better but later quality dropped due to heavy rains and much of the wheat has had to be stored in silos and dried," Prostran said.

Average yield was around 3.8 tonnes per ha, ranging from 2.5 tonnes per ha in Montenegro, with a wheat area of just over 2,200 ha, to over 4.0 tonnes in the granary region of Vojvodina where more than 356,000 ha were sown to wheat.
Total domestic needs are estimated at 2.4 million tonnes.
"This indicates we will have a realistic surplus of 300,000 to 500,000 tonnes for possible export," Prostran said.
But a decision on exports should not be hasty as the country could be brought into a situation to have to import wheat, he added.
Yugoslavia had to import around 300,000 tonnes of wheat earlier this year after exporting some 450,000 tonnes in 1996.
"I personally feel the size of exports should be decided only after final balances are drawn and after fall sowing is completed," Prostran said.
Prostran said it was positive the wheat market has started reviving a little this year and that there were no administrative limits to other organisations besides the state trading in wheat.
"Milling and baking organisations are directly involved now as well as the Federal Commodity Reserve Agency which was fairly passive in past years," he said.
The Federal Commodity Reserve Agency earlier this week invited a tender for 15,000 tonnes of new wheat.
The Serbian Commodity Reserve Agency is otherwise very active, buying up most of the country's wheat for its reserves.

This year's seed wheat production of around 130,000 tonnes against last year's 80,000 tonnes guarantees more area will be sown in the fall with declared seed which will ensure higher yield and quality, Prostran said.
The chamber said some 30,000 to 40,000 hectares of wheat were damaged by cold weather, hail and rainstorms.
"This translates into some 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes of lost crop," Prostran said.
"We must sow between 800,000 to one million hectares if we want to satisfy domestic needs and become a permanent exporter of around one million tonnes of wheat."
